Football Players Are Leveraging NIL Paydays to Buy Million-Dollar Homes
 
Plus, a custom-built house for under $1 million and how stainless-steel design became more expensive—and somehow hotter—than ever
 
By Kerry Barger
 
 
CREDIT: STEVE CRAFT FOR WSJ
 

This is an edition of the WSJ Homes newsletter, a weekly guide to luxurious properties, celebrity homes, interior design and the housing market. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 

My days of dorm living are far behind me, but I remember them like it was yesterday. Cramped quarters. Communal bathrooms. The mini fridge that didn’t smell quite right.

 

Noah Fifta got a taste of the dorms early on in his college career, but now the University of Arizona football player lives in a renovated, four-bedroom house with mountain views and a pool about 3 miles from campus. Property records show he bought the Tucson, Ariz., home last year for $950,000.

 

Football players used to wait until reaching the NFL to consider buying a home, but a 2021 rule change allowing college athletes to profit from their fame has sped up that timeline. Player pay has surged, creating a multibillion-dollar market in Name, Image Likeness, or NIL, payments. Starters on major college football teams now earn hundreds of thousands—or even millions—of dollars a year.

 

Flush with cash, many college football players are jumping into the real-estate market and buying homes in their university towns.

 

“This can change our lives forever,” said Fifita, 23, a fifth-year player.

 
 
Noah Fifita at his house in Tucson. CREDIT: STEVE CRAFT FOR WSJ
 

It’s getting trickier to build a custom, architect-designed home for less than seven figures, but one North Carolina couple managed to do it for $700,000. Here’s what they built.

 

Finally, we look at why stainless-steel home goods and furniture have become trendier than ever, despite a price increase of up to 45%.

How Two Retirees Pulled Off a Custom-Built Home for Under $1 Million

 
 
JEREMY M. LANGE FOR WSJ
 

They cut square footage by skipping a garage and eliminating hallways, but didn’t skimp on their yoga studio.

 
 
 

What’s the Deal?

 
 
HARRIS ALLEN
 

Tech entrepreneur Parker Conrad is the buyer of a $43 million estate on Martha’s Vineyard that just set a Massachusetts sales record. Conrad is co-founder and CEO of Rippling, an AI-driven workforce-management platform based in San Francisco that was valued at $16.8 billion after a 2025 funding round.

 

A castle-like home set on roughly 80 acres is coming on the market in Iowa for $10.2 million. The circa-1990s house is the most expensive for sale in the state.

 

A contemporary San Francisco home built for art collectors located in the South Park neighborhood is asking $11.5 million. Its unusual, industrial design has made it a landmark for Pokémon Go players.

 

Want to see more deals? Sign up for our Mansion Deals email alert to have the biggest and best luxury home sales and listings delivered to your inbox.

 
 
 

The Luxe Life

 
 
AUSTIN JOHN
 

Once reserved for appliances, industrial kitchens and medical supplies, stainless steel is now featured in sought-after luxury design shops—becoming the first homegoods phenomenon to buck President Trump’s tariffs.

 

Judith Light was just about to quit acting when her therapist told her to stick with it. “The moment I walked out his door, my pager buzzed. I was cast as an understudy on the soap opera ‘One Life to Live.’”

 
 
 

House of the Week

 
 
RETOMEDIA
 

A red pickup truck inspired one couple to buy our latest House of the Week on Oregon’s Sauvie Island.

 

Peter Stott had long wanted a 1950 Chevy pickup with two doors and five windows. When his wife, Julie Stott, bought him one for his 70th birthday, they decided they needed a farm to go with it. They purchased 26.66 acres and spent $8 million building a two-level home.
